title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 91
paragraphs: There are many other offerings by Croesus in Greece beyond those I have already mentioned. At Thebes in Boeotia, he dedicated a golden tripod to Ismenian Apollo. At Ephesus, there are the golden cows and most of the temple pillars. In the temple of Athena Pronaia at Delphi, there is a large golden shield. These were still in place in my own time. Other offerings have been lost. His offerings at Branchidai in Milesian territory were, I am told, equal in weight and similar in kind to those at Delphi. The gifts he sent to Delphi and to the shrine of Amphiaraos came from his own wealth, the first-fruits of his inheritance. But the other offerings were made from the property of an enemy—a man who had conspired against Croesus before he became king, trying to make Pantaleon ruler of Lydia instead. Pantaleon was a son of Alyattes and half-brother to Croesus, but by a different mother: Croesus was born to a Carian woman, Pantaleon to an Ionian. When Croesus won the kingdom by his father's choice, he executed his rival by drawing him across a carding comb. The man's property, which Croesus had earlier vowed to dedicate, he offered to the shrines I have named. That is enough about his offerings.
